definition.text: Discounting is the arrangement in which someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time.

facts.text: The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle the debt.
Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects.
A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest.
The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for the income the money could have earned by being invested meanwhile.
Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn in other assets of similar risk over the same period.
Discounting is tied to the time value of money: a payment has a different future value and present value.
Discounting turns a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value.

definition.text: The discount rate is the rate at which the charge for delaying a payment must grow as the delay gets longer.

facts.text: The discount yield is the share of the original debt that must be paid to delay payment for one year.
In financial calculations the discount rate is usually set equal to the cost of capital.
The rate may be adjusted upward to allow for the risk that expected cash flows will not arrive.
Start-up firms are typically given higher discount rates than established companies, reflecting disadvantages such as hard-to-sell shares and few willing investors.
The capital asset pricing model builds a discount rate as the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity market risk premium.
The risk-free rate is the return from investing in risk-free securities such as government bonds.

definition.text: A discount factor is the number a future cash flow is multiplied by to get its present value.

facts.text: It is computed from a zero (spot) rate taken from a yield curve and the time in years until the cash flow.
Banks usually discount cash flows with daily compounding, because accrued interest on their assets can be re-lent every day.
For hand calculation, continuous compounding is sometimes a close enough approximation to daily compounding.
In dynamic decision models, impatience is represented by a discount factor between 0 and 1.

definition.text: Hyperbolic discounting is a model of how people devalue delayed rewards in which their choices are not consistent over time.

facts.text: Under hyperbolic discounting, value falls quickly over short early delays but more slowly over longer delays.
In an early study, people were indifferent between $15 now and $30 in 3 months, $60 in 1 year or $100 in 3 years: implied yearly discount rates fell from 277% to 139% to 63%.
By contrast, exponential discounting lowers value by a constant factor per unit of delay, so the discount rate stays the same.
Many people take $50 now over $100 in a year, yet almost everyone picks $100 in six years over $50 in five years, though it is the same trade-off.
Its key consequence is temporary preferences for smaller, sooner rewards over larger, later ones, so people make choices their future selves regret.
It is described by the discount factor g(D) = 1/(1 + kD), where D is the delay and k sets how strongly rewards are discounted.
Preference reversals were first found in rats and pigeons, so the effect does not depend on human culture.
It is one of the cornerstones of behavioral economics and has been used to study retirement saving, credit-card borrowing, addiction and procrastination.

title: Uncertain hazard as a source of hyperbolic discounting

definition.text: One explanation of hyperbolic discounting is that a future reward carries a risk of not arriving, and that risk is uncertain.

facts.text: A restaurateur offered $100,000 in sixty years instead of $50 today would reasonably discount it, since the payer or payee may have died.
If the hazard rate of losing the reward is unknown and given a prior distribution, the expected survival probability of the reward takes exactly the hyperbolic form.
Whether discounting future gains is rational, and at what rate, depends greatly on circumstances.

definition.text: Quasi-hyperbolic or beta-delta discounting is a discrete-time approximation of hyperbolic discounting proposed by Laibson in 1997.

facts.text: It uses two constants, beta and delta, each between 0 and 1, with delays counted in whole periods.
Rewards taken now are not discounted at all.
It keeps much of the mathematical convenience of exponential discounting while capturing the main feature of hyperbolic discounting.

title: Criticism of hyperbolic discounting

definition.text: Researchers have proposed several alternative explanations for the non-exponential discounting that hyperbolic models describe.

facts.text: Daniel Read's subadditive discounting holds that discounting over a delay grows when the delay is split into smaller intervals.
The most obvious objection is that many people learn to choose consistently over time in most situations.
A 2014 paper criticised studies for relying mostly on university students and concluding too quickly that the hyperbolic model is correct.
Human experiments often show wide differences between subjects.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether hyperbolic discounting, a similarity heuristic or subadditive discounting best explains observed choices.

title: Social discount rate

definition.text: The social discount rate is the discount rate used to value money spent on public or social projects.

facts.text: It puts a present value on costs and benefits that come later, and it is critical when costs and benefits are spread unevenly over a long time.
It is used to value projects such as highways, schools or environmental protection, where future costs include maintenance and future benefits include reduced pollution.
A higher social discount rate makes a social project less likely to be funded.
A small rise in the rate can matter enormously for benefits far in the future.
The US Office of Management and Budget recommends about 7% as a pretax return on private investment, while HM Treasury sets 3.5% for the UK public sector.
Developed nations typically use lower rates (3–7%) than developing nations (8–15%).
It reflects how a society values well-being today against well-being in the future.
Economists have no consensus and no one-size-fits-all choice of rate, owing to national variations.

contested_note: The choice of social discount rate is a long-running and fierce debate among economists, sharpened by the Stern Review.

definition.text: Frank Ramsey's formula builds the social discount rate from pure time preference plus the elasticity of marginal utility times the growth rate of consumption.

facts.text: The formula's inputs are time preference, the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption and the economic growth rate.
If future generations will be richer, a positive discount rate reflects the diminishing marginal utility of consumption.
The Stern Review let its discount rate vary with outcomes, reflecting growth and the elasticity of marginal utility, in line with Ramsey's growth model.

title: Pure time preference debate
article: Social discount rate#"Pure time preference" debates

definition.text: Pure time preference is the assumption that an experience, or a life, is intrinsically worth more the sooner it occurs, and whether society should use it is disputed.

facts.text: Philosopher Toby Ord says most philosophers think pure time preference lacks moral justification, and Frank Ramsey called it ethically indefensible.
Derek Parfit compared it to an indefensible spatial discount rate that would care less about effects per yard of distance.
Andreas Mogensen argues a positive rate can be justified by kinship, since common-sense morality lets us favour those closer to us.
Over long spans a fixed rate becomes counterintuitive: 1% would mean Tutankhamun should value one day of his life above all lives today.
When asked about the welfare of others rather than their own, most people's apparent pure time preference shrinks or vanishes.
Critics warn that weighting future generations fully can lead to a 'Pascal's mugging' conclusion that present welfare barely matters.

contested_note: Economists commonly include pure time preference, while most philosophers reject it and some defend it on kinship grounds.

title: Discounting in climate economics
article: Social discount rate#In global climate change

definition.text: The choice of discount rate for the benefits of cutting greenhouse gas emissions is a highly controversial question in climate economics.

facts.text: The Stern Review of 2006 warned that global GDP risked a 20% cut unless 1% of world GDP was invested now to reduce global warming.
Critics objected that its findings partly rested on an extremely low pure time preference rate of 0.1%.
It is a common misconception that the Stern Review used a zero discount rate: its projections used many positive rates while taking time preference near zero.
Discount rates in climate cost–benefit analysis range from zero to over 3%.
A rival model with a 3% rate declining to 1% over 300 years found carbon taxes necessary but much smaller than Stern recommended.
Under Obama the US social cost of carbon was $51/ton at a 3% discount rate; Biden proposed over $190/ton using lower rates.

contested_note: Some argue giving future generations less weight is ethically indefensible, others that equal weighting yields nonsensical results.
